clue.text: Those with good memories get saddled with them

definitions.text: Those with good memories get saddled with them

parts.words: Those with good memories get saddled with them
parts.note: elephants are said never to forget, and in India they carry seats strapped to their backs for riders

explanation.surface: People with sharp memories end up burdened with something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Those with good memories' sounds like clever people; it is elephants, who proverbially never forget, and 'saddled' is literal: the seat sits on the elephant's back.
explanation.definitionFit: A canopied seat for riding on an elephant's back is what elephants are fitted with.

clue.text: Unfortunate chap just keeps his head ?

definitions.text: Unfortunate chap just keeps his head ?

parts.words: Unfortunate chap just keeps his head
parts.note: an unlucky man who barely escapes with his life, and also the word chap with its head taken away

explanation.surface: An unlucky man narrowly escapes execution.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is CHAP without its head plus LESS: chap minus C, a man who did not keep his head.
explanation.definitionFit: Hapless means unlucky, the condition of an unfortunate man.

clue.text: Licensing hours notwithstanding, you can always get a drink in the country

definitions.text: Licensing hours notwithstanding, you can always get a drink in the country

parts.words: Licensing hours notwithstanding, you can always get a drink in the country
parts.note: the country's name has a beer, ale, inside it, whatever the pub opening times

explanation.surface: Whatever the pub laws, the countryside always offers a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Licensing hours were the legal pub opening times; ALE sits inside the country's name, though that country was famous for its dry Sundays.
explanation.definitionFit: A country of Britain whose name has a beer inside it.

clue.text: Fair game, this old lady

definitions.meaning: a fairground throwing game, and so also a target for everyone's criticism
the target is the head of an old woman figure, named as a relative

explanation.surface: This old woman is a legitimate target.
explanation.walkthrough: At British fairs players threw sticks to knock a pipe from the mouth of a wooden old woman's head; the name came to mean anyone set up to be attacked.
explanation.definitionFit: The fairground game targets a figure of an elderly woman, and the term now means a person set up for criticism.

clue.text: Drawing-rooms?

parts.note: rooms where artists do their drawing, not formal parlours

explanation.surface: Formal parlours in a grand house.
explanation.walkthrough: A drawing-room is a parlour; read literally it is a room for drawing in.
explanation.definitionFit: Artists' workrooms are where drawing is done.

clue.text: The least one can do, to make the car silent

parts.note: the Mini is a small British car
mum means saying nothing, as in 'keep mum'

explanation.surface: Doing the bare minimum to quieten a noisy car.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mini is the classic small British car; 'mum' is British for silent, as in 'mum's the word'.
explanation.definitionFit: The smallest possible amount of effort is the least one can do.

clue.text: Big enough to get on terms with

indicators.note: to get suggests the letters of on terms produce a new word by rearrangement

explanation.surface: Someone is large enough to compete on equal footing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get' rearranges ON TERMS; 'enough' and 'with' only fill out the picture of being on equal terms.
explanation.definitionFit: Something huge and enormous is monster-sized.

clue.text: More fastidious

parts.note: an old sense of a common word meaning pleasant: fussy and particular

explanation.walkthrough: The everyday word for pleasant also means precise or particular, as in 'a nice distinction'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nice in its older sense means particular or fussy, so this comparative means fussier.

clue.text: They serve to keep a body clean, on the road

definitions.text: They serve to keep a body clean, on the road

parts.words: They serve to keep a body clean, on the road
parts.note: a body read as a car's bodywork, kept free of splashes while driving

explanation.surface: Things that help a traveller stay washed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a body' sounds like a person; it is a vehicle's bodywork, shielded from road splashes.
explanation.definitionFit: Curved guards over wheels stop dirt spraying onto a vehicle.

clue.text: Two companies or three's one, perhaps, thanks to them

definitions.text: Two companies or three's one, perhaps, thanks to them

parts.words: Two companies or three's one, perhaps, thanks to them
parts.note: after combinations of firms, two or three businesses become a single one

explanation.surface: Twisting the saying that two's company and three's a crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface plays on 'two's company, three's a crowd'; combining businesses makes several companies one.
explanation.definitionFit: Corporate combinations unite separate firms into a single company.

clue.text: Its user can't bear it

parts.note: the passenger of this covered litter does not carry it: bearers do the carrying

explanation.surface: Someone cannot stand a thing they use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can't bear it' suggests dislike; literally the rider cannot carry the litter, which needs bearers.
explanation.definitionFit: A covered litter carried on poles by bearers is used by a passenger who is carried, not carrying.

clue.text: It grows in a nice dark situation

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the words 'nice dark', spanning the gap between them

explanation.surface: A plant that thrives in a pleasant, shady spot.
explanation.walkthrough: The tree is in 'niCE DARk'; 'a' and 'situation' just round off the picture of where it grows.
explanation.definitionFit: A cedar is a tree, something that grows.

clue.text: Stops decapitation — relaxes

indicators.note: cutting off the head means the first letter of the word for stops is removed

parts.note: ceases means stops

explanation.surface: Beheadings are halted and the tension lifts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'decapitation' removes the head, C, from CEASES.
explanation.definitionFit: To ease off is to relax, so eases means relaxes.

clue.text: With which an idle tuner might take a spell

definitions.text: With which an idle tuner might take a spell

indicators.note: to spell the words idle tuner anew is to rearrange their letters into another word

explanation.surface: A musician resting during a break in the music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spell' reads as a rest period, and it is one, but it also tells you to respell IDLE TUNER.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical break between acts gives a performer a rest period.

clue.text: Medicaments from a pie-fancier

definitions.meaning: herbal remedies made from a single plant were called by this name
Simple Simon of the nursery rhyme wanted the pieman's pie, so things from him belong to Simple

explanation.surface: Medicines handed out by someone who loves pies.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme Simple Simon met a pieman and wanted to taste his wares, so the pie-fancier is Simple, and things of his are Simple's.
explanation.definitionFit: Old herbal medicines were single-herb preparations; and the possessive of Simple Simon's name fits 'from' him.

clue.text: Roman dame makes notes

indicators.note: makes signals that the letters of Roman dame are formed into something else

explanation.surface: A Roman lady writes some notes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes' rearranges ROMAN DAME.
explanation.definitionFit: Memoranda are written reminders, notes.

clue.text: Prizes cause open hostility among Communists

indicators.note: one set of letters is placed in the middle of the word for Communists

parts.note: Reds is a common name for Communists
war is hostility out in the open

explanation.surface: Awards stir up conflict among the Party faithful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'among' puts WAR inside REDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Rewards are prizes given for achievement.

clue.text: It's a stick-up — by an interior decorator !

definitions.text: It's a stick-up — by an interior decorator !

parts.words: It's a stick-up — by an interior decorator
parts.note: stick-up read as something pasted up on a wall, not a robbery

explanation.surface: A robbery carried out by a home decorator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stick-up' sounds like an armed robbery; it is paper pasted onto a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: Decorative paper pasted onto room walls is what a decorator sticks up.

clue.text: Asiatic who may reform some day

indicators.note: may reform suggests the letters of some day will be rearranged

explanation.surface: An Asian person who might mend their ways one day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may reform' rearranges SOME DAY; the Samoyed are a people of northern Siberia.
explanation.definitionFit: The Samoyed are a people of Siberia, so one of them is an Asian.

clue.text: U-boats' fuel under the bed ?

parts.note: U-boats are German submarines, subs
oil is a fuel

explanation.surface: Submarine fuel kept hidden beneath someone's bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bed' is a flower bed or soil bed: the layer below the topsoil.
explanation.definitionFit: The layer of soil beneath the topsoil lies below a garden bed.

clue.text: Ball-boys for instance ?

parts.note: ball read as a dance, so the boys at it are those dancing

explanation.surface: Boys who fetch tennis balls.
explanation.walkthrough: Ball-boys fetch tennis balls; here they are boys at a ball, a formal dance.
explanation.definitionFit: People at a ball take to the floor and dance.

clue.text: A wet type — if a good cat-pacifier?

definitions.meaning: a feeble, unmanly person, a wimp
a piece of bread soaked in milk would keep a cat quiet

explanation.surface: A drip of a man who could at least calm a cat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wet' is British for feeble; the second reading splits the word into its two parts: a sop dipped in milk, ideal for a cat.
explanation.definitionFit: A feeble, timid man is a weakling; and a sop soaked in milk soothes a cat.

clue.text: Arms of fictitious comrades-in-arms

parts.note: the weapons carried by Dumas's trio of royal guardsmen, whose name comes from them

explanation.surface: The limbs of invented soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: Dumas's heroes take their title from their guns; 'Arms' means weapons, not limbs.
explanation.definitionFit: The firearms of Dumas's guardsmen gave them their name.

clue.text: Departs in confusion — it's the gate-crashers !

indicators.note: in confusion signals that the letters of Departs are jumbled

explanation.surface: Uninvited guests leave in a muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in confusion' rearranges DEPARTS. Gate-crashers sound like party intruders; petards were bombs used to blow in castle gates.
explanation.definitionFit: A petard was a small bomb used to blow open gates, so petards break gates down.

clue.text: It's about one to a bar with these singers

indicators.note: to means added on after the bar

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: about means the letters of It's go round the word one

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe giving no letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A singer counts out one beat to each bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts ONE inside ITS to give ITONES, and 'to' attaches that after BAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Singers with voices between tenor and bass are a class of male vocalists.

clue.text: Number of novel users of 19 dn.

definitions.text: Number of novel users of 19 dn.

parts.words: Number of novel users of 19 dn.
parts.note: how many title characters in the Dumas novel carry those guns

explanation.surface: A count of the people using a new gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' sounds like 'new'; it is Dumas's book, named after its trio of guardsmen.
explanation.definitionFit: Dumas's book names its heroes as a trio, so the count is the number after two.

clue.text: Shelley wrote of a sensitive one

definitions.text: Shelley wrote of a sensitive one

parts.words: Shelley wrote of a sensitive one
parts.note: Shelley's poem about a mimosa in a garden has this title, 'The Sensitive ...'

explanation.surface: The poet Shelley wrote about a delicate soul.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a sensitive one' sounds like a person; Shelley's poem is about a mimosa.
explanation.definitionFit: Shelley's poem is titled after a sensitive mimosa, a growing thing in a garden.

clue.text: " Drowned in a bath Of the tresses of ——" (Poe)

definitions.text: Drowned in a bath Of the tresses of

parts.words: Drowned in a bath Of the tresses of
parts.note: a line from Poe's poem addressed to a woman, missing her name

explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap: the line comes from Poe's poem 'For ...', addressed to the woman named at its end.
explanation.definitionFit: Poe's poem is addressed to a woman of this name, whose hair the line describes.

clue.text: You can't say he hasn't got something

definitions.text: You can't say he hasn't got something

parts.words: You can't say he hasn't got something
parts.note: a person who possesses a thing plainly has it, so no-one can deny he has something

explanation.surface: A grudging compliment: the man has some quality after all.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase usually concedes some charm or talent; literally it describes a possessor.
explanation.definitionFit: A possessor holds property, so he certainly has something.

clue.text: It means exposure for the pupils

definitions.text: It means exposure for the pupils

parts.words: It means exposure for the pupils
parts.note: pupils read as the dark centres of the eyes, laid open to the light

explanation.surface: A revelation that teaches schoolchildren something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pupils' looks like schoolchildren; they are the eye's pupils, exposed when the lids part.
explanation.definitionFit: A revelation, something surprising, literally uncovers the eyes.

clue.text: They are responsible for fixing charges

definitions.text: They are responsible for fixing charges

parts.words: They are responsible for fixing charges
parts.note: charges read as explosive charges or cartridges put into guns, rather than prices

explanation.surface: Some officials set the prices people pay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fixing charges' sounds like setting prices; here it is putting charges into guns or mines.
explanation.definitionFit: People who load guns or blasting charges put the explosive in place.

clue.text: Mail order workers?

parts.note: people at the post office who put the mail in order by destination

explanation.surface: Staff at a catalogue shopping firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mail order' suggests catalogue shopping; these workers put the mail in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Post-office staff who arrange letters by destination organise the mail.
